claims.text: Conventional sputtered AlCoCrFeNi HEA multilayer coatings have fully crystalline interfaces.
Modified sputtering using a low-energy gas pulse or reduced substrate temperature during interface deposition can form stable, nanometer-thick amorphous interfacial regions in AlCoCrFeNi multilayers.
The modified coating will contain amorphous interfacial regions between crystalline HEA layers.
TEM and XPS can verify the formation and testing-condition stability of the proposed amorphous interfacial layers.
The lack of long-range order in the amorphous interfacial layers reduces the availability of dislocation-nucleation sites.
Amorphous interfacial layers impede dislocation transmission across interfaces.
Reduced dislocation nucleation and interfacial transmission delay the initiation and propagation of dislocation motion under prolonged stress.
Delayed dislocation motion reduces creep-strain accumulation.
Relative to fully crystalline multilayers, amorphous-interface coatings will accumulate less creep strain over time.
Relative to fully crystalline multilayers, amorphous-interface coatings will require a higher threshold load to initiate plastic deformation.
The proposed improvement should apply during nanoindentation creep from room temperature through 200 degrees Celsius.
At higher temperatures or very high stresses, amorphous-layer instability may eliminate the proposed creep-resistance mechanism.
The amorphous interfaces may crystallize or degrade during prolonged high-stress or higher-temperature exposure.
Modified and fully crystalline control coatings should be compared under identical constant-load nanoindentation creep tests from room temperature through 200 degrees Celsius.
The comparison should measure creep strain versus time, threshold load for plastic-deformation onset, and post-test interfacial phase stability.
A lack of statistically significant creep-strain reduction or threshold-load increase relative to the crystalline control would falsify the hypothesis.
Post-test crystallization or instability of the amorphous interfaces would falsify the hypothesis.
